problems.stem: You prompt Codex to scaffold an interactive flashcard widget for your prototype. It generates working code that stores all card data in a single global variable and hardcodes the answers in the HTML. As an instructional designer, what is the first thing to evaluate?
options: Whether the code runs without errors, since that is the only thing that matters.
Whether the generated structure supports the learning interaction you designed, such as separating content from logic so non-coders can edit cards and so answers are not exposed to the learner.
Whether the variable names match a style guide.
Whether Codex used the newest JavaScript syntax.
problems.explanation: Codex optimizes for code that runs, not for instructional or maintainability requirements. The designer evaluates whether the structure serves the intended learning interaction and authoring workflow.

problems.stem: Which prompt to Codex reflects sound design-first authoring rather than handing over the design decision?
options: "Make me a good quiz for my module."

"Generate a 5-item single-select quiz component that shows per-item feedback immediately, keyboard-navigable, with answers stored separately from the markup; I will write the items and feedback text."
"Build whatever quiz you think works best and pick the questions too."
"Write a quiz and make it look impressive."
problems.explanation: The strong prompt specifies the learning interaction and constraints the designer already decided, leaving Codex to implement, not to make the pedagogical choices.

problems.stem: Codex suggests adding an animated confetti burst every time a learner answers, including on wrong answers. What is the strongest bounded response?
options: Keep it, because positive feedback is always motivating.

Reject it for wrong answers and reconsider its frequency, since celebrating errors and constant animation can mislead learners and add extraneous load; accept the suggestion only where it supports the learning goal.
Remove all feedback animations to be safe.
Ask Codex whether the confetti is pedagogically sound and follow its answer.
problems.explanation: An AI authoring suggestion is a proposal to judge against learning goals. Confetti on wrong answers conflicts with accurate feedback, so the designer accepts it selectively or rejects it.

problems.stem: After Codex generates your prototype's scoring logic, you notice it marks an answer correct only if the casing matches exactly. Which revision note best documents an evidence-based fix?
options: "Codex used a case-sensitive string match; I changed it to normalize case and trim whitespace because learners typed 'Paris' and 'paris' and both are correct, verified against three test inputs."
"Asked Codex to improve scoring and accepted the result."
problems.explanation: A strong revision note names what the generated code did, what you changed, the learner evidence that motivated it, and how you verified it. Vague notes leave the decision unauditable.
